# Lambda Labs GPU Pricing 2026: Per-Hour Rates

Fazlur Rahman September 23, 2026· Updated October 27, 2026 7 min read

Lambda Labs GPU pricing 2026: H100 PCIe 1x at $3.29/GPU-hr; H100 SXM 1x at $4.29/GPU-hr; H100 SXM 8x at $3.99/GPU-hr; B200 SXM 8x at $6.69/GPU-hr; A100 PCIe 40GB at $1.99/GPU-hr. Lambda 1-Click Cluster reserved pricing starts at $5.54/GPU-hr at 256-GPU scale. Lambda bills per-minute with no egress fees.

Last verified: Sep 16, 2026.

...

> - Cheapest published GPU: Quadro RTX 6000 at $0.69/GPU-hr (legacy visualization)
> - Cheapest AI GPU: A100 PCIe 40GB at $1.99/GPU-hr; V100 16GB at $0.79/GPU-hr
> - H100 PCIe 1x: $3.29/GPU-hr; H100 SXM 1x $4.29/GPU-hr
> - H100 SXM 8x: $3.99/GPU-hr (208 vCPUs, 1.8 TB RAM, 22 TB SSD per node)
> - B200 SXM 8x: $6.69/GPU-hr; B300 not listed on-demand
> - 1-Click Cluster reserved: 16-GPU HGX H100 $6.16/GPU-hr; 256-GPU $5.54/GPU-hr
> - Egress: Free; billed per-minute; no setup fees

...

## On-Demand Cloud pricing breakdown

Lambda On-Demand Cloud publishes per-GPU-hour rates for 10 GPU SKUs with explicit instance configurations.

Verified July 2026 (lambda.ai/instances):

- Quadro RTX 6000 (24 GB, 14 vCPUs, 46 GiB RAM, 512 GiB SSD): $0.69/GPU-hr — legacy visualization card
- Tesla V100 (16 GB, 88 vCPUs, 448 GiB RAM, 5.8 TiB SSD): $0.79/GPU-hr
- RTX A6000 (48 GB, 14 vCPUs, 100 GiB RAM, 512 GiB SSD): $1.09/GPU-hr
- A10 (24 GB, 30 vCPUs, 226 GiB RAM, 1.3 TiB SSD): $1.29/GPU-hr
- A100 PCIe 40GB (40 GB, 30 vCPUs, 225 GiB RAM, 512 GiB SSD): $1.99/GPU-hr
- A100 SXM 80GB (80 GB, 240 vCPUs, 1.8 TB RAM, 19.5 TiB SSD): $2.79/GPU-hr on 8x
- GH200 (96 GB, 64 vCPUs, 432 GiB RAM, 4 TiB SSD): $2.29/GPU-hr
- H100 PCIe 1x (80 GB, 26 vCPUs, 225 GiB RAM, 1 TiB SSD): $3.29/GPU-hr
- H100 SXM 1x (80 GB, 26 vCPUs, 450 GiB RAM, 5.5 TiB SSD): $4.29/GPU-hr
- B200 SXM6 8x (180 GB, 208 vCPUs, 2.9 TB RAM, 22 TiB SSD): $6.69/GPU-hr
- B200 SXM6 1x (180 GB, 26 vCPUs, 360 GiB RAM, 2.75 TiB SSD): $6.99/GPU-hr

Lambda's B300-class hardware is not yet listed on the On-Demand Cloud card (the homepage mentions GB300, B300, B200, H200 infrastructure for larger deployments, but self-serve pricing is still pending). For B300 access the path is 1-Click Cluster reservation or sales engagement.

## 1-Click Cluster reserved pricing

Lambda 1-Click Cluster reservations unlock 30-40% off equivalent on-demand rates — and guarantee capacity for the reservation window.

Verified July 2026 (lambda.ai/pricing):

- HGX H100 16-GPU: $6.16/GPU-hr (2-week to 1-year)
- HGX H100 64-GPU: $5.85/GPU-hr
- HGX H100 256-GPU: $5.54/GPU-hr
- HGX B200 16-GPU: $9.86/GPU-hr
- HGX B200 64-GPU: $9.36/GPU-hr
- HGX B200 256+ GPU: $8.87/GPU-hr
- 1-year+ reservation (both H100 and B200): Custom — Talk to our team

1-Click Clusters are invoiced on separate terms from On-Demand Cloud — weekly increments under reservation terms, with explicit GPU count and duration negotiated at approval. The 256+ tier delivers 32% off the on-demand 8x H100 rate ($3.99/GPU-hr x 1.55x volume multiplier); the 16-GPU reservation tier delivers 54% off on-demand because Lambda amortizes the deployment cost across a fixed GPU count.

results.title: Data center GPU price: published rates, dates and sources
results.author: Dora Pruteanu
highlights:
In short

A data center GPU has no single price: an H100 rents at $5.191 per accelerator-hour on AWS Capacity Blocks, $3.99 per GPU-hour on Lambda, and $2.82 on the SemiAnalysis market index (April 2026). This guide separates list, street and contract price and shows which vendors publish none.

...

- AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks lists an H100 at $5.191 per accelerator-hour in US regions; a B200 is $12.355; AWS has announced new rates from 7 October 2026.
- Lambda rents an on-demand H100 SXM at $3.99 per GPU-hour; 1-Click Clusters run $6.16 at 16 GPUs down to $5.54 at 256.
- H100 1-year rental contracts rose from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026, per SemiAnalysis.
- On-demand H100 capacity has been marked sold out on the SemiAnalysis index from February to April 2026.

## What data center GPUs cost right now

Three published figures answer the question as of 23 September 2026, each from a different price layer. AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML lists the NVIDIA H100 at $5.191 per accelerator-hour in US regions and the B200 at $12.355 per accelerator-hour, with new reservation rates announced effective 7 October 2026 [1]. Lambda lists an on-demand H100 SXM instance at $3.99 per GPU-hour and a B200 SXM6 at $6.69 per GPU-hour [2]. The SemiAnalysis H100 spot-contract composite index, a weighted mean of observed rental prices across the market, stood at $2.82 per GPU-hour in April 2026 [3].

...

- List price: the on-demand rate a provider publishes on its own pricing page, such as Lambda's $3.99 per H100 GPU-hour [2].
- Street price: what market indices observe buyers actually paying. The SemiAnalysis H100 spot-contract composite index is built from hyperscale clouds, neoclouds, marketplaces and rental aggregators, weighted toward hyperscalers.
- Contract price: reserved or committed terms. AWS Capacity Blocks carry a reservation fee plus an operating system fee, and reservation prices are updated regularly with supply and demand.

Over the past year the contract layer moved sharply upward. SemiAnalysis reports H100 one-year rental contract pricing rising almost 40 percent, from a low of $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 per GPU-hour by March 2026, with on-demand rental capacity sold out across all GPU types in early 2026 [4]. Those are point figures from the launch article; the same firm's index history publishes the one-year term as a 25th-75th percentile range, which ran $1.45-2.00 in November 2025 and widened to $2.10-2.70 in April 2026, with the on-demand H100 row marked sold out from February through April 2026 [3]. The two starting figures are not in conflict: one is a survey-based point estimate, the other a percentile band from the scraped-market index.

...

Combine dated rental tiers with index ranges rather than single points. Lambda's 1-Click Clusters price an H100 at $6.16 per GPU-hour for 16 GPUs, $5.85 at 64 and $5.54 at 256, showing the scale discount a single spot figure hides [2]. The SemiAnalysis one-year H100 contract range of $2.10-2.70 per GPU-hour in April 2026 is a different layer from the same page's spot-contract composite index level of $2.82 [3].

...

On AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks an H100 rents at $5.191 per accelerator-hour in US regions and a B200 at $12.355, with new rates announced effective 7 October 2026. Lambda lists an on-demand H100 SXM at $3.99 and a B200 SXM6 at $6.69 per GPU-hour. Over the past year, H100 1-year rental contracts rose from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026 per SemiAnalysis, and on-demand H100 capacity was marked sold out on the SemiAnalysis index from February to April 2026.

results.title: Lambda raises $1B, gets investment grade ratings from ...
results.author: Mike Canevaro
highlights:
Lambda raised $1B against its GPUs — and landed investment grade ratings from Morningstar DBRS and Moodys. A first for this market (I think). That unlocks insurance and bond money at under 7%, instead of banks charging high-yield rates near 9%. GPUs financed like infrastructure, not hardware. Did the AI buildout get a bigger wallet?

...

**Reshared from James Howl-Newton:**
> Lambda has raised $1 billion of debt against GPUs, and the detail that matters most is the credit rating. Morningstar DBRS gave it A (low) and Moody's Ratings gave it Baa1. Both are investment grade. For GPU-backed financing, that is new.
>
> Up to now, most of the debt funding the AI build has been high yield, priced in the mid-7s to 9% to cover the risk. This facility came in at a 6.78% fixed rate, was oversubscribed, and was marketed to insurance companies and fixed income investors rather than banks. That is a different, deeper and cheaper pool of capital, and it only opens up once the paper carries an investment-grade stamp.
>
> The loan is secured on two things, the GPU servers themselves and the contracted cash flows from the customers using them. Those customers are two investment-grade offtakers across several data centres, and spreading the revenue across more than one strong name is part of what earned the rating. Customer concentration has been the main worry hanging over this kind of lending, and this deal answers it by diversifying the offtakers inside a single financing.
>
> A few of the other features are textbook infrastructure finance rather than tech lending. It is a delayed-draw loan, so Lambda only pulls down capital as each cluster is commissioned and starts earning, which avoids paying interest on money it is not yet using. It runs to 2033 and fully amortises, so the principal is paid down steadily over the life of the loan instead of in one lump at the end. Long-dated, secured, amortising, contracted. This is GPU debt built to behave like a power station rather than a piece of equipment.
>
> Offtakers, contracted cash flows, an investment-grade rating, insurance buyers. All of it treats compute as long-life infrastructure rather than fast-depreciating kit. It is the clearest sign yet that GPU financing is maturing from a speculative, high-yield corner into something the most conservative institutional money will own.
>
> Be realistic about where it sits though. A 6.78% coupon is still well above what a genuine blue-chip borrower pays, so the market is pricing in real technology and obsolescence risk even at investment grade. The rating also leans on those offtakers staying strong and the contracts holding. But the direction of travel is clear, and for Lambda this is the third new credit market it has opened in 18 months, building the kind of debt track record that sits nicely alongside its reported move toward an IPO.
>
> Structuring and pricing deals like this takes genuine expertise.
>
> If you're looking to hire that kind of talent, get in touch.

Cloud rental hasn’t followed retail. GetDeploying’s rental price index, which tracks 81 providers, is up 4.9% over the past 12 months, a small change next to a 5070 that’s 46% over MSRP. Most of that increase is on the newest datacenter chips. AIMultiple’s index shows the latest-generation GPUs up 123% since October 2024, while mid-range “modern” GPUs rose 7% and older generations dropped 46%. RTX 4080 rental prices were flat over the last 90 days.

As of September 17, 2026, the median on-demand RTX 4090 across 20 providers tracked by GetDeploying was $0.45 per GPU-hour (AIMultiple has it at $0.44). The RTX 5090 median was $0.67/hr, and the H100 median was $3.39/hr. For comparison, H100s regularly rented for more than $7 an hour in early 2024.

# Lambda Labs Alternatives for Teams Outgrowing GPU Rental 

 NoraLin 358 2026-10-16 03:55:02 Edit 

OneSource Cloud is a managed private AI infrastructure provider that enterprises evaluate when Lambda Labs (now branded Lambda) on-demand rental no longer fits steady training, regulated data, or multi-team operations. Lambda Labs alternatives span hyperscalers, marketplace GPU clouds, specialized cluster providers, and dedicated managed private infrastructure. This page maps when each class fits, with break-even math and migration steps.

...

## What Lambda Offers Today

Lambda has grown from a deep learning hardware company into a GPU cloud with three tiers of service. At the time of writing (as of October 2026), its public pricing page lists:

| Service | What it is | Public price examples (as of Oct 2026) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On-demand instances | Self-serve single-node GPU instances, first-come access | H100 SXM 80 GB at $3.99 per GPU-hour; B200 at $6.69; A100 80 GB at $2.79 |
| 1-Click Clusters | Self-serve multi-node clusters from 16 to 2,000+ GPUs, two-week minimum | B200 at $9.86 per GPU-hour for 16 GPUs, $9.36 for 64, $8.87 for 256+ |
| Superclusters (private cloud) | Single-tenant rack-scale clusters with InfiniBand for very large deployments | Contract pricing |

Lambda also provides Lambda Stack for drivers and frameworks, managed Kubernetes and Slurm, and states SOC 2 Type II and several ISO certifications. Prices change; verify on the provider site before budgeting.

...

One 8-GPU H100 instance at Lambda's list price of $3.99 per GPU-hour costs:

- Per month, running continuously: 8 × $3.99 × 730 hours ≈ $23,300
- Per year: 8 × $3.99 × 8,760 hours ≈ $279,600

results.title: Neocloud pricing climbs while AI inference costs fall — TechReaderDaily
results.author: M Mireille Otsuka Staff reporting
highlights:
Now read it against the other half of the stack. Inference, the thing those GPUs are increasingly rented to do, is deflating at the per-token level. Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform, shipping to eight named cloud partners including CoreWeave and Lambda, is marketed around what TechTimes described as 10x lower token cost and roughly triple the memory bandwidth per part. Ten times is a marketing figure until someone publishes the batch size, sequence length, and SKU it was measured on. But directionally, the cost of producing a token is falling on a schedule that has nothing to do with the price neoclouds are signing today.

...

The upward leg is not subtle. Nebius raised major GPU prices 17% to 21%, and short-duration capacity negotiations have reached $40 million to $50 million per megawatt, per Seeking Alpha's September analysis. CoreWeave signed new compute capacity contracts at higher prices in the third quarter of 2026, adding $25 billion in commitments. Set those against the Vera Rubin roadmap and you have a three-year contract written at 2026 prices for hardware that will produce tokens at a fraction of 2026 cost. That is a good trade for a seller with a backlog and a bad trade for a buyer who signed without a price-reset clause.

results.title: The neocloud credit cycle: what broke on October 14, 2026 — Jesse Hawkins
results.author: Jesse Hawkins
highlights:
Less than eight hours after the U.S.

...

My claim in this article is that the AI trade now has a credit layer under it that did not exist two years ago, and that this credit layer set the price on October 14. Demand for GPUs is as strong as it has ever been. Rental prices are rising, CoreWeave’s CEO said in August that its near-term capacity “remains effectively sold out,” and Nebius raised its on-demand GPU prices by about 20% on average on October 1. The change came in the price of the money that turns that demand into data centers.

...

The same split shows up across the industry. Lambda’s $926 million term loan, backed by an unnamed investment-grade offtaker, priced at SOFR + 300 and was rated Baa2 in August. IREN financed its Microsoft contract with $3.65 billion of loans rated A by Fitch at a blended 6.0%. Nebius’s first secured facility, $775 million in July, priced at SOFR + 250 against an investment-grade customer’s contract.

...

Debt priced on an investment-grade customer costs about 6%; debt priced on the neocloud costs 8.5%–10% at issue and about 15% in the secondary market on October 14. The convertible coupon is low because buyers are also paid in equity volatility. Sources: company 8-Ks and releases (CoreWeave, IREN, Nebius, Lambda, Galaxy), New York Fed (SOFR). IREN's ~9% rate is from a single secondary source.

...

Every neocloud’s revenue rests on a short list of customers. In the first half of 2026, CoreWeave’s largest customer was 40% of its revenue and the second was 23%. Nscale’s IPO filing showed 52% of first-half revenue from one customer. Lambda’s backlog rose from $15 billion in June to $50 billion in September, mostly on a $35 billion commitment from Anthropic. Concentration on customers rated A or better, as Microsoft, Meta and Google are, makes the financing cheap, and concentration on AI labs makes it expensive.

...

Anthropic’s position is similar but newer, and in the last quarter it became the anchor tenant of the second tier: Lambda ($35 billion), Nscale ($45 billion for a West Virginia campus, per Nscale’s filing), TeraWulf (a 20-year lease worth about $19 billion, expected to be supported by investment-grade credit), and, by press reports, Fluidstack. Anthropic’s revenue has grown faster than any software business I know of, and its commitments have grown faster still.

...

The GPU renters (CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda, Nscale) own the chips and sell compute by the hour or by the contract. They carry the full risk of GPU obsolescence and repricing. Nebius has financed itself mostly with convertibles. Its August deal raised $5.75 billion with the purchasers’ options at coupons of 0.50% and 4.50% with conversion prices near $313 and $325, against a stock that now trades at $186. Its customer prepayments are also large. It expects more than $9 billion of them in 2026, and about 70% of its landmark Q2 deals included prepayments covering 50–60% of the related capex, according to its Q2 shareholder letter. A prepayment is customer-provided financing at a zero coupon, and it is the cheapest money in the industry. Nebius’s converts are now deep out of the money, so its next raise will price more like debt than equity.

...

The private companies are under the same pressure. Firmus, an Australian neocloud with Meta and OpenAI contracts, cancelled a planned IPO of about $5 billion on the Australian Securities Exchange, announced October 9, after cutting its price from A$11 to A$9 a share. Nscale filed for a New York listing in September at a valuation target of up to $35 billion and is still waiting. Lambda moved its IPO to 2027 and is raising up to $4 billion privately. These are the cases CoreWeave’s CEO meant when he wrote that difficulties and delays at some rivals’ IPOs and debt financings “are bleeding into the narrative around CoreWeave,”.

results.title: Nvidia Flags 15% NVL72 Price Hike as Memory Spot Prices Climb Sevenfold — Chip Dispatch
results.author: Nathan Brooks
highlights:
Nvidia Flags 15% NVL72 Price Hike as Memory Spot Prices Climb Sevenfold — Chip Dispatch

# Nvidia Flags 15 Percent NVL72 Hike As Memory Spot Prices Climb Sevenfold

Nvidia has warned NVL72 buyers of a 15 percent price hike next year as Objective Analysis' Jim Handy briefed Hot Chips 2026 on a memory market where spot prices have climbed sevenfold.

By

Nathan Brooks

October 12, 2026

## Key specs

- Nvidia warned buyers of a 15 percent price increase on Grace-Blackwell and Vera-Rubin NVL72 systems for next year, per Bloomberg at Hot Chips 2026
- Objective Analysis' Jim Handy cited a sevenfold rise in memory spot prices on a shared DRAM, NAND, and HBM production base
- GPU components are sold out for 2026 with allocations locked through the end of 2027
- Broadcom is now the third-largest HBM buyer behind Nvidia and AMD, driven by its custom XPU business
- Memory shortages tied to AI demand are forecast to persist through at least 2030

Nvidia has informed buyers of its Grace-Blackwell and Vera-Rubin NVL72 rack-scale systems of a 15 percent price increase next year. The warning surfaced via Bloomberg at the Hot Chips 2026 conference, where the memory market set the tone for the week.

Hyperscalers and cloud builders have absorbed nearly every available GPU component for 2026, with allocations largely locked through the end of 2027. Smaller system vendors now have little leverage in a market where the largest buyers set the terms.

...

Broadcom and Marvell can compete for HBM capacity on price on behalf of those smaller customers who would otherwise miss the queue. Nvidia has reportedly inserted flexible pricing provisions into contracts so it can pass rising memory costs to ODMs, OEMs, and ultimately to system buyers. A 15 percent list-price increase looks almost modest given the sevenfold rise Handy cited on the spot market.
